impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations in 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe tolling, and whether a prior Federal Circuit decision on this issue was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's ANZ Securities decision.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501's statute of limitations is not subject to American Pipe tolling, recognizing that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's California Public Employees' Retirement System v. ANZ Securities, Inc. The court affirmed dismissal of breach of contract and Fifth Amendment takings claims filed by bank holding company and subsidiaries that lost assets during the 2008 financial crisis.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity for government defendants that the six-year limitations period for Court of Federal Claims actions is a firm deadline not subject to class action tolling, reducing exposure to stale claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Businesses and investors who relied on class action filings to toll limitations periods for government claims will find their individual claims time-barred if not independently filed within the statutory period.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a trial court must defer to the terms of an existing license agreement when assessing copyright infringement damages, and whether the court improperly applied the 'book of wisdom' doctrine to assess non-compensatory damages against the government.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that courts are not compelled to defer to existing license agreement terms when calculating copyright infringement damages via a hypothetical negotiation, but vacated the $12.68 million damages award in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' and assessed non-compensatory damages. The case involved the government's unauthorized copying of TETRA® software used for military healthcare interoperability.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders benefit from the ruling that courts may use hypothetical negotiation frameworks rather than being locked into pre-existing license terms, potentially yielding higher damages in infringement cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: The ruling that post-infringement evidence (the 'book of wisdom') cannot be used to justify non-compensatory damages limits copyright holders' ability to inflate damage awards beyond actual losses.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations had expired for Insulet's Defend Trade Secrets Act claim against EOFlow for misappropriating trade secrets related to insulin patch pump technology through hiring of former employees.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict and damages award in favor of Insulet, holding that the DTSA statute of limitations had expired before Insulet filed suit in 2023. EOFlow had hired former Insulet employees who shared CAD files and proprietary information about the Omnipod insulin pump in 2018, but the court found Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing. The permanent injunction was also reversed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's three-year limitations period, providing a firm defense where the plaintiff delayed filing suit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face significant risk of losing claims if they do not promptly investigate and file suit upon learning of potential misappropriation, even when the full scope of harm is not yet known.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages models measuring the defendant's enrichment and in reducing the jury's breach of contract damages award.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models, while reversing the reduction of the jury's breach of contract award and reinstating it. The court affirmed Ford's liability for misappropriating Versata's automotive configuration software trade secrets under both the DTSA and Michigan law. The case involved Ford developing its own competing software (PDO) while licensing Versata's software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret owners benefit from the ruling that unjust enrichment damages models should be considered in DTSA/state trade secret cases, potentially broadening available damages theories. The reinstatement of the jury's breach of contract award also supports upholding jury damages determinations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal alternatives while licensing third-party software face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk and potentially broader damages exposure under enrichment-based theories.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' in a provisional patent application to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in the non-provisional application constituted a correctable obvious typographical error, entitling the patent to claim priority from the provisional application.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating all claims of Enanta's patent covering compounds for inhibiting coronavirus replication, holding that the change from C2 to C1 in the chemical substituent definition was not an obvious typographical error correctable to maintain priority. Without the earlier priority date, Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (the active ingredient in Paxlovid®) anticipated the patent claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers and competitors benefit from strict enforcement of provisional application support requirements, preventing patentees from expanding claim scope beyond what was originally disclosed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical companies and patent applicants face severe consequences from even minor drafting errors in provisional applications, as they cannot later broaden scope to capture competitors' intervening disclosures.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds that were not included in its IPR petition, and whether the court adequately accounted for hindsight bias in its analysis.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve, finding insufficient evidence to estop one invalidity ground and that the court failed to adequately account for hindsight bias in estopping the other. The case involved Valve's Steam Controller and a video game controller patent with back controls, clarifying the standard for when prior art references 'reasonably could have been' discovered by a skilled searcher.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ruling requiring courts to rigorously evaluate whether prior art could reasonably have been discovered without hindsight, preserving more invalidity defenses in district court after IPR proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face a higher burden to invoke IPR estoppel, as courts must now more carefully assess whether prior art references were truly discoverable through diligent pre-IPR searching.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain exclusionary rights—including the right to sue for infringement—have sufficient Article III standing even after granting an exclusive license. The court found the retained right to sue was not rendered illusory by the license terms, which also gave the patentee approval rights over sublicensing and assignment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring licensing agreements can retain standing to enforce their patents against third parties by carefully reserving the right to sue, providing flexibility in enforcement strategies even with exclusive licensees.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face broader exposure to patent infringement suits from both licensors and licensees when license agreements are structured to preserve the licensor's independent enforcement rights.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and whether the district court properly denied judgment as a matter of law on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of eligibility for two patents while affirming eligibility for two others, affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, and remanded for further proceedings. The case involved patents on non-uniform constellation designs used in digital broadcast communication systems incorporated into LG televisions, with a jury verdict of willful infringement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies with patents on concrete improvements to communication systems (such as specific constellation designs) benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for some claims, supporting patent protection for practical innovations in wireless communications.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face continued uncertainty under § 101, as the court vacated eligibility determinations for certain claims, requiring further analysis and potentially limiting protection for related inventive concepts.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a verdict form that asks a single infringement question covering multiple patents is reversible error, and whether the district court erred in its § 101 eligibility analysis under Alice step two for wireless building automation system patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, finding that the single-question verdict form covering all asserted patents was prejudicial error because the jury found one patent invalid but still returned a general infringement verdict without identifying which patents were infringed. The court also vacated and remanded the § 101 analysis for the '495 patent while affirming eligibility for the '887 and '371 patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement for patent-specific infringement questions on verdict forms, preventing general verdicts that obscure which patents support liability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders pursuing multi-patent litigation must ensure verdict forms separately address each patent, and a flawed verdict form can result in complete vacatur of damages even where some infringement findings are upheld.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming relay devices and methods for automated capture, processing, and sharing of farming operation data are directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in declining to find the case exceptional under § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's patents on automated farming data collection systems were patent-ineligible under § 101, finding the claims directed to the abstract idea of collecting, processing, and sharing data using generic computer components. The court vacated the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional under § 285, remanding for reconsideration of Farmers Edge's attorneys' fees request.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies facing patent assertions based on data collection and processing claims benefit from continued rigorous application of § 101, reducing exposure to suits based on abstract-idea patents with generic implementations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Agricultural technology companies and other businesses holding data-processing patents face continued vulnerability under § 101 and increased risk of exceptional-case fee awards when asserting patents found ineligible.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a pharmaceutical patent's weight-to-weight ratio limitation, and whether the court permissibly waived the Rule 65(c) bond requirement for a preliminary injunction pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction preventing Hetero from launching a generic competitor to Nuedexta (treating neurological disorders), upholding the district court's construction of disputed claim terms. However, the court vacated the waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement, holding that the district court must require Otsuka to post a bond pending appeal to protect Hetero from wrongful injunction damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance of the preliminary injunction, supporting enforcement of pharma patents against generic entrants near patent expiration.
impacts.negativeImplications: Preliminary injunction plaintiffs cannot avoid posting a Rule 65(c) bond pending appeal even when equities strongly favor injunctive relief, ensuring generic manufacturers have financial protection against wrongful exclusion from the market.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence where the petitioner's expert testimony was conclusory, and whether a third party may file an IPR petition timed to the one-year deadline of a different party's litigation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's finding that all challenged claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent were unpatentable as obvious, finding the Board's reliance on conclusory expert testimony insufficient. Qualcomm had filed the IPR petition on the exact deadline applicable to Roambee (the actual litigant against FedEx), raising concerns about surrogate IPR petitions. The court remanded for further proceedings on obviousness.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from heightened scrutiny of conclusory expert testimony in IPR proceedings and from the court's skepticism of third-party petitioners acting as surrogates to challenge patents in coordination with actual litigants.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to use IPR proceedings to challenge competitors' patents face greater evidentiary burdens, and surrogate filing strategies may face increased judicial scrutiny.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of International Trade erred in sustaining Commerce's remand determination that debt-to-equity conversions conferred no countervailable benefit, where Commerce's original determination found a subsidy existed.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and reinstated Commerce's original determination that debt-to-equity conversions by a Korean steel manufacturer constituted countervailable subsidies. The court found Commerce's protest-based remand determinations—finding no benefit—were unsupported, and ordered reinstatement of the original countervailing duty findings against Dongbu Steel.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel producers and manufacturers benefit from the reinstatement of countervailing duties, supporting fair competition against foreign producers receiving government subsidies through debt-to-equity conversions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign manufacturers and importers face renewed countervailing duty exposure when government-backed debt-to-equity conversions are found to confer benefits, even after Commerce issued favorable remand determinations under protest.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claim terms reciting 'executable program code configured to' perform functions should be construed as means-plus-function terms under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), in light of the intervening precedent in Dyfan, LLC v. Target Corp.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling on the '978 patent and remanded for reconsideration of whether 'executable program code configured to' limitations invoke § 112(f) means-plus-function treatment under the framework established in the court's intervening Dyfan decision. The court affirmed the invalidity judgment on the '638 patent based on anticipation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders benefit from the opportunity to argue against means-plus-function treatment of 'executable program code' claim language under evolving Federal Circuit precedent, potentially saving claims from indefiniteness.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers who obtained indefiniteness rulings based on means-plus-function interpretations of software claims may see those rulings reconsidered under the more nuanced Dyfan framework.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement complaint with prejudice on obviousness grounds based on an IPR decision invalidating related claims, and whether the case qualified as exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285 or warranted attorney sanctions under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of the patent infringement complaint on obviousness grounds but reversed both the § 285 exceptional-case fee award against the patent holder and the § 1927 sanction against its counsel. The court found insufficient grounds to conclude the case was exceptional or that counsel acted in bad faith merely by asserting surviving claims after related claims were invalidated in IPR.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders and their counsel benefit from the ruling that asserting surviving patent claims after IPR invalidation of related claims does not automatically render a case exceptional or support attorney sanctions, protecting access to courts.
